nodes.label: command-policy.ts Design
nodes.rationale: evaluateCommand is a pure, I/O-free function over an ordered deny-rule table with no container knowledge, deliberately isolated so it is unit-testable with a table of allow/deny command strings — the core 'backend policy decision' the rubric wants to see tested in isolation.

nodes.label: item.started vs item.completed Timing Confirmation
nodes.rationale: Whether the engine achieves prevention or only fast containment depends on whether Codex's item.started carries the command before it finishes executing. The implementation checks the policy at whichever event first reveals the command text, so it automatically gets the best available timing without a redesign once confirmed; claims in the README/demo were deliberately scoped to 'terminated immediately, blocking continuation' rather than 'zero bytes ever reach the destination' until this was verified live.

nodes.label: Command Policy Engine
nodes.rationale: Layered as shell-parse.ts -> capabilities.ts -> command-policy.ts so a rule is a statement about capabilities (e.g. an actor holding SECRET_READ may not also exercise NETWORK_EGRESS) rather than a pattern over shell syntax, so many command spellings collapse into one rule, evidence reports what was attempted rather than which regex matched, and the same rules can later govern non-shell actions like an MCP tool call or database write.

nodes.label: Defect: Environment Protection at Wrong Layer
nodes.norm_label: defect: environment protection at wrong layer
nodes.rationale: A whitespace-boundary regex over command text denied harmless commands like 'echo env' while treating 'printenv | grep ARK_API_KEY' as safe; enumerating every equivalent dump (env, Node, Python, nested shells, /proc) cannot create a sound text-level boundary. Fixed by moving protection to the generated Codex config's shell_environment_policy exclude, which filters ARK_API_KEY before command spawn, keeping generic env/process.env/os.environ inspection allowed while explicit dereferences and /proc/.../environ reads remain denied as defense in depth.

nodes.label: Defect: Filename Denylist Masked attacker.example
nodes.rationale: A file-extension denylist added so index.d.ts is not read as a domain included 'example', which masked every attacker.example host in the corpus and silently re-opened three previously-caught attacks. It was introduced while fixing another finding and reduced detection silently, including for the live demo's primary attack host — the scorecard caught it on the next run.

nodes.label: Defect: Unblocked Bare Reverse Shell
nodes.rationale: The /dev/tcp/ egress rule only escalated when paired with a named secret, and host extraction could not read a host out of a /dev/tcp/ path, so a bare reverse shell with no secret named fell through every branch; the existing test only covered /dev/tcp/ combined with a secret read, so the gap was invisible until the corpus harness found it. Fixed by extracting hosts from raw-socket paths.

nodes.label: Approval Safety Design Choice
nodes.rationale: Only the egress rules (network-egress-denied, network-egress-denied-implicit) are reviewable because they sometimes hit a legitimate need such as a package registry; secret-exfiltration and protected-secret-access are always hard-denied so no operator can be socially engineered or fatigued into approving theft of a protected secret. A granted exception is scoped to the exact hosts consumed by a single run, proven live by a second task to the same host being held again — approval is never a standing allowlist change.

nodes.label: Named Operational Gaps
nodes.rationale: Four honest gaps: policyEvents/approvals logs accumulate forever with no retention or access rule (redacting secrets into a log that is never bounded is the second privacy problem the discipline warns about); the policy assumes a fixed runtime image and model with nothing to re-trigger evaluation when either changes; 'approver' is a free-text name, not an authenticated principal, since this POC has no identity system; and only held (reviewable) runs can be reconsidered — a secret-exfiltration block is final by design with no appeal.

nodes.label: Deployment Secret Handling
nodes.rationale: Ark keys configure model access while Volcengine account AK/SK configures Terraform, and account AK/SK must never be passed to an Agent Runtime; .env.production, terraform.tfvars, and Terraform state must not be committed. The POC still stores the Ark key in Terraform user data and state, so production deployments require managed secrets and an encrypted remote state backend.

nodes.label: Exfiltration Guard Implementation Plan
nodes.rationale: Chose an application-level policy engine over a network-level sandbox (custom Docker networking / iptables egress allowlisting) because it is pure Node.js, needs no changes to container capabilities, and behaves identically across Docker, Colima, and rootless Podman — the three engines the Starter Kit must support. The residual risk that a single command can start executing before it is observed and reacted to is documented explicitly rather than hidden, as the acceptance checklist requires.

nodes.label: Defect: bash -lc Quote-Wrapping Bypass
nodes.rationale: Every real Codex command is reported wrapped as /bin/bash -lc '<command>', so the real binary is preceded by a quote rather than whitespace; every egress rule used a word-boundary regex that did not include quote characters, so against real traffic the egress rules matched nothing. Attacks naming a secret still tripped protected-secret-access, which hid the gap: the flagship demo appeared to work but via the wrong rule. Fixed by adding quote characters to every boundary class.

nodes.label: Known Bypass: base64-encoded eval
nodes.rationale: eval "$(echo <base64> | base64 -d)" encodes the entire command so nothing incriminating is literal in the command text, defeating any text-matching control. Only network-layer egress restriction fully closes this class; it was deliberately not attempted in favor of a portable, pure-application-layer control that works identically across Docker, Colima, and rootless Podman. Recorded in the corpus deliberately rather than hidden.

nodes.label: OWASP Agentic Design Principle (Propose vs Authorize)
nodes.norm_label: owasp agentic design principle (propose vs authorize)
nodes.rationale: The LLM proposes an action; a deterministic trusted component authorizes it. Model output, retrieved documents, and tool results are all untrusted when they can influence a consequential command, so the model cannot bypass the gateway by phrasing a command differently — every consequential path reaches the same enforcement point.

nodes.label: Sentinel Known Limitations
nodes.rationale: Detection is textual so a fully base64-encoded command defeats it; containment is a race against a fast single command completing before teardown, not a guarantee zero bytes leave; the guard is a reactive command-text check, not a network allowlist, so implicit destinations (bare npm install, git push to a preconfigured remote) pass; and policy state lives in a single-writer JSON store with no retention bound. Recorded honestly because each is a real gap.

nodes.label: Pull Request Guidelines
nodes.rationale: PRs must explain the behavior and reason for the change, add tests for API/lifecycle/persistence/Runtime changes, update English docs and .env.example when configuration changes, and never commit credentials, local state, workspaces, build output, or Terraform state — keeps a three-day hackathon codebase focused, reproducible, and reviewable.

nodes.label: Security Known Limitations
nodes.rationale: A shared demo token with no user identity, authorization, RBAC, or tenant isolation; no CSRF protection; no per-Agent container boundary in ECS mode; ordinary (not hardened multi-tenant) sandboxes; broad outbound network access; prompt-triggered command/file execution; and the Ark key available to the server, active Runtime container, and Terraform state — documented so users scope the POC correctly rather than assume production hardening.

nodes.label: Safe Use Guidance
nodes.rationale: Use a dedicated/disposable host, a scoped and revocable Ark key with a unique APP_AUTH_TOKEN, keep local use on loopback and restrict ECS CIDRs, add HTTPS before sending the shared token over an untrusted network, never mount production data or provide account AK/SK to Agents, and destroy resources/revoke keys after the event — mitigations sized to a single-user hackathon POC, not production hardening.

nodes.label: Credential Boundary (ARK_API_KEY exclusion)
nodes.rationale: Generated Codex configuration keeps ARK_API_KEY available to the model provider but excludes it from spawned shell commands, and Codex's default KEY/SECRET/TOKEN exclusions remain enabled, so generic env/process.env/os.environ inspection stays usable without disclosing credentials; explicit Ark-key dereferences and /proc/.../environ reads are separately denied as defense in depth.
